workshops.title: Instruments: save a trace and inspect one interval
workshops.summary: Record one scratch action and inspect its time range and sampled stack. Investigate surviving objects separately, using actual saved traces for observations and clearly labeled invented excerpts for practice.

simple.story: You watch someone make lunch and take a photo every few moments. In one photo, they are peeling an apple. That photo belongs both to making lunch and to peeling. Counting it once for lunch and once for peeling would count the same observation twice. The photos also cannot tell you the exact number of times the peeler moved. They help you notice where work happens. A stopwatch answers elapsed time, while looking in the cupboard afterward answers which objects are still there. Each tool answers a different question.
simple.meaning: Time Profiler samples stacks. An inclusive sample includes work in a frame's descendants; a self sample belongs to the frame itself. Elapsed time and object retention require their own evidence. A supplied synthetic stack is practice material, not a captured device trace.

example.before: The invented MapRows interval runs from 2.000 to 2.160 seconds and contains 80 main-thread samples. The mapper has 64 inclusive samples and 4 self samples.
example.change: Separate the mapper's own samples from the samples in its descendants.
example.after: 60 samples are in descendants, and 4 + 60 = 64 inclusive samples. The remaining 16 of the 80 lie outside that mapper subtree. These counts are neither invocation counts nor exact milliseconds.

picture.caption: An actual investigation needs capture, interval selection, stack interpretation, and a separate confirmation experiment.

words.meaning: A saved recording of observed activity from a particular process and environment.
An app marker that helps locate a named event or interval in a recording.
One profiler observation of what a thread was executing.
Samples attributed to a frame together with work below it in the call stack.
Samples attributed to the frame itself, excluding its descendants.
References that explain why an object is still kept alive.

simple.remember: Select one operation, then use the right evidence for CPU work, elapsed time, and retained objects.
simple.boundary: Photos explain sampling and double-counting, not precise profiler timing. A short or waiting operation can have few CPU samples. Synthetic counts establish no device performance result, and a Memory Graph snapshot differs from an allocation history. A real trace still needs matching symbols and a controlled confirmation run.

sections.title: Choose one action and its expected result
sections.html:
A trace is a saved recording of activity in a chosen process. Before collecting one, name the operation you want to explain. That is the same useful habit you bring from Android's Perfetto. Use the isolated SwiftUIWorkbench app with its synthetic Gallery, UIKit, Stores, and Platform tabs. Choose one Gallery navigation or UIKit list action. Write the start action and the expected end state so you can find the same operation later in the recording. Keep permission prompts and real services outside that first capture. Three tiny cards may reveal no hotspot; the first run can still teach you how to collect and save evidence.

For a mapping investigation, the supplied CapturePlan.swift contains a deliberately simple stable-first-occurrence scan and a MapRows signpost. It is a separate teaching file, not automatically included or invoked by the app. In your own scratch copy, add it to the app target and call it from a practice action. Construct a frozen array outside the call, retain its returned value, and check complete ordered output afterward. That makes the measured operation meaningful and keeps fixture construction out of a mapping-only interval.

Record source revision, fixture size and duplicate pattern, app configuration, destination, installed Xcode/Instruments version, and whether this is a simulator or phone. Do not infer a Release build from the Profile button: inspect the scheme’s Profile action. A simulator capture can explain that environment; product latency, rendering, thermal, and energy conclusions need the appropriate representative device evidence.

sections.title: Record, stop, and save a real trace
sections.html:
Time Profiler samples what threads are executing. Open the scratch project, verify its app scheme and destination, and use the native lab instructions to build and install when available. Start Product → Profile, or attach Instruments to that installed scratch process. Record which method you used: attaching after launch misses the earlier preparation. Select Time Profiler for sampled CPU work. If available in your installed tool, add the signpost or points-of-interest view to locate named app intervals. Template names can differ by version. Check the capabilities you need: stack sampling and an identifiable operation interval.

Start recording, perform one declared operation, wait for its defined completion, and stop. Avoid a long session containing unrelated browsing, background work, and repeated fixtures. Confirm the intended process and a visible recording timeline before interpreting anything. If MapRows is absent, inspect target membership, whether the action actually called the function, subsystem/category filtering, and the selected process. The presence of the Swift source alone proves no interval ran.

Save the trace with the fixture and environment ledger. Keep matching executable and symbols available; an unattributed address cannot support a precise source claim. Record failed setup and missing tracks explicitly. You have completed a recording only after the tool actually produced the saved artifact. This course includes a procedure and synthetic interpretation excerpts, not a preexisting device trace.

sections.title: Limit the timeline before counting samples
sections.html:
An interval is the start-to-end time range for one operation. Select the single MapRows interval, or the exact action range you declared. Limit the call tree to that range, then inspect the main thread separately from worker threads. Elapsed time measures how long the operation took from start to end. CPU samples observe executing work. An async operation may spend much of its elapsed time waiting or suspended, with little CPU sampled. A long interval therefore does not prove expensive synchronous Swift code. A very short operation may produce few samples, so a missing visible stack is weak evidence too.

The supplied diagnostic excerpt invents an interval from 2.000 to 2.160 seconds and eighty main-thread samples. The mapper contains sixty-four inclusive samples but only four self samples. Its descendants account for the rest. These are synthetic counts, not milliseconds or invocation counts. Inclusive cost contains child work; self cost attributes samples to the frame itself. Adding a parent’s inclusive count to its child’s count double-counts the same observations.

Try an inverted call tree to find a common expensive leaf and compare it with the ordinary caller path. Preserve the selected interval, thread filter, and any hidden-system-library filter in the report. A whole-process percentage can change merely because unrelated work changed. Keep the interpretation local: this selection supports a repeated-membership hypothesis, which still needs an equivalent candidate and matched confirmation measurements.

sections.title: Use the stack to form a testable explanation
sections.html:
A call stack shows the chain of functions involved in sampled work. Follow it from the scratch action into captureStableMapping, membership searches, and String comparison. One possible mechanism is repeated scanning as output grows. That explanation predicts more work as input size and duplicate patterns change. It must still preserve complete output and first-occurrence order. Check competing explanations: fixture creation inside the interval, sorting, image decoding, or layout outside the mapper. A source function's name does not show which mechanism dominated the recording. Write a prediction that a controlled experiment could disprove.

Record one representative expanded stack and its symbol identity. If the selected range contains mostly waits, use the appropriate activity, networking, or scheduling evidence instead of claiming the mapper consumed CPU. If the main thread is busy but the user-visible delay lies elsewhere, a mapping optimization may not improve the intended endpoint. Keep first-frame presentation, default launch-metric boundaries, and product readiness separate, as lesson 037 requires.

A candidate experiment can substitute set-backed membership while comparing complete expected output, not just result count. Collect diagnostic traces to explain the mechanism, then confirm the primary latency with comparable, minimally instrumented runs. Profiling overhead and a changed fixture can distort a before/after result. Do not invent a percentage improvement from this synthetic stack or treat one trace as a stable tail distribution.

sections.title: Find what keeps an object alive after leaving a screen
sections.html:
A retaining path is a chain of references keeping an object alive. CPU samples do not explain that lifetime. Start a separate Allocations recording. Mark a baseline generation, enter and leave the chosen route, then mark another generation so you can group allocations around that action. Repeat a small fixed number of cycles and inspect newly created instances still alive afterward. Compare them with the intended owner lifetime before calling them leaks: a cache may keep an object deliberately. Temporary peak memory and objects retained after route exit also answer different questions.

The optional RetentionFixture.swift intentionally stores a closure that strongly captures its own instance. Add it only to a learner scratch experiment. Keep one route-owned reference, invoke it, then remove that reference. The synthetic ownership graph is instance → stored callback → closure context → instance. A weak observer can confirm survival without retaining it, and the supplied stop method breaks the stored edge. The file’s expected-value check demonstrates this small ARC contract when run.

For an actual retaining path, attach Xcode’s debugger to the same scratch process and capture Memory Graph after route exit. Select the surviving instance, follow incoming strong references, and distinguish a cycle from a still-live legitimate owner. The graph is a stopped snapshot, not an Allocations history. Break the intended ownership edge in your scratch copy, repeat the same route cycles, and verify behavior and retention. Weak capture must still deliver the required callback semantics.

sections.title: Label captured, predicted, synthetic, and pending evidence
sections.html:
An evidence packet is the material another person needs to check your claim. Include the saved trace, matching app identity, environment, selected interval, expanded stack, operation contract, expected-value checks, and any memory ownership notes. Mark fields observed, predicted, synthetic, or pending. A Time Profiler capture supplies no retaining path by itself. A host weak-reference assertion supplies no device footprint or Memory Graph capture. If a graph shows a cache root, explain the cache's intended budget and invalidation rule before proposing removal. Every conclusion should point to the kind of observation that can support it.

A useful first conclusion is narrow: “The selected interval contains synchronous repeated membership checks; their effect on action-to-usable content remains unmeasured.” Another is “The deliberately cyclic fixture survives owner removal and releases after stop; actual app ownership still needs a captured path.” Either can guide the next experiment without claiming a production defect.

Android trace markers resemble signposts as operation labels, but their APIs, frame boundaries, and tooling views differ. Allocations history and Memory Graph complement each other rather than mapping exactly to a Java heap dump. Ask a peer to reopen one saved interval and reconstruct one retaining path. Missing setup becomes a concrete documentation gap, while unexecuted device work remains an explicit next task.

exercise.brief: Save one short Time Profiler trace in a learner copy of the scratch app. Investigate one object's lifetime separately. Attach your observations and mark unavailable tool or device steps pending.
steps: Write the operation's start and end, fixed fixture, Profile configuration, and destination before recording.
If using MapRows, add CapturePlan.swift to your own scratch app target, call it from one synthetic action, and check the complete returned values.
Record the action, stop, and save the trace. Select its interval and distinguish self samples from inclusive samples without adding both.
Run a separate, fixed number of route-entry and route-exit cycles for Allocations. When available, capture Memory Graph and follow the actual strong references.
Label the optional cyclic fixture as a deliberate experiment. Repeat after stop, check callback behavior and lifetime, and record which observations remain pending.
acceptance: Process, configuration, fixture, trace and selected interval are identifiable.
Sample counts are not reported as invocation counts or exact elapsed milliseconds.
CPU, allocation history, graph ownership and product latency are separate claims.
Synthetic excerpts and unexecuted device steps remain labeled.
No client source, production account or learner completion is changed.
exercise.solution:
Choose one MapRows call with a fixed duplicate-containing array. Start the interval immediately before the synchronous mapper and end it when the returned value is available. Check complete ordered output outside the interval. In the invented excerpt, 4 self samples plus 60 descendant samples make the mapper's 64 inclusive samples; they must not be added again as 68. Set-backed membership is a candidate only if it preserves the full expected output and receives comparable confirmation runs. The synthetic stack establishes no measured saving.

The memory answer follows the deliberately stored callback cycle. A weak observer sees the instance after the route-like strong owner is cleared; calling stop removes the callback and permits release. For an actual report, attach the route-cycle generation and graph edges, then repeat under the same lifetime policy. Allocation count alone does not identify the owner. The final ledger leaves phone responsiveness, peak footprint, energy, and any uncaptured graph pending. Learners supply their own trace and results; the example never records course completion.

quiz.question: What does a mapper’s inclusive sample count include?
options: Only instructions directly in the mapper
Samples attributed to the mapper and its descendants in the selected range
The exact number of calls made
quiz.explanation: Inclusive samples contain child stacks. Self samples isolate attribution to that frame; neither is an exact invocation count.

quiz.question: After a route exits, what identifies an unexpected owner?
options: The app’s total memory figure alone
A file containing the class declaration
A captured incoming strong-reference path for the surviving instance
quiz.explanation: The ownership graph supplies the actual retaining edges. A memory total or source file cannot identify who retains one object.

quiz.question: A short simulator trace shows repeated membership checks. Which conclusion is supported?
options: A mechanism hypothesis for that captured operation and environment
An observed physical-device launch improvement
A lower fleet p95
quiz.explanation: The trace supports local attribution. Device outcomes and fleet distributions require their own comparable measurements.

workshops.title: Artifact debugging: match settings, resources, and symbols
workshops.summary: Investigate an unexpected build branch, a missing resource, and mismatched crash symbols. Follow declarations into resolved settings and existing products, keeping invented excerpts separate from observed artifacts.

simple.story: A shop has several boxes labeled Model Train. Each train also has a small serial number underneath. You find an instruction booklet with the same cover name, but it was printed for another serial number. The title looks right, yet its wiring diagram may describe a different train. Before using it, you match the exact model and serial number. A label on a box tells you what someone called it. Opening the box and reading the marks on the actual train tells you what you have.
simple.meaning: An app name, scheme label, or source declaration is not enough to identify a built artifact. Effective settings explain selected behavior; packaged contents explain resources; crash, executable, and dSYM UUIDs identify which symbols can describe a binary.

example.before: The synthetic arm64 crash image and executable have UUID 11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555. The offered dSYM has UUID AAAAAAAA-BBBB-CCCC-DDDD-EEEEEEEEEEEE.
example.change: Compare the relevant UUID and architecture before interpreting the crash address.
example.after: The UUIDs differ, so the offered dSYM cannot establish that function's identity. Locate the matching retained artifact; a matching app name does not repair the mismatch.

picture.caption: Three pieces of the invented crash case must agree on identity before precise symbol attribution.

items.label: Executable
items.text: Its relevant arm64 UUID matches the crash image.

items.label: Offered dSYM
items.text: Its AAAAAAAA-BBBB-CCCC-DDDD-EEEEEEEEEEEE UUID does not match.

items.label: Diagnosis
items.text: Precise address attribution remains blocked pending matching symbols.

words.meaning: A concrete build product or retained file, such as an executable or symbol bundle.
A selected Xcode operation, such as Run or Profile, with its own configuration choice.
The final setting after selected declarations and overrides have been resolved.
The target or bundle responsible for packaging and looking up a resource.
A debug-symbol bundle describing a particular built binary.
An identifier used here to match a binary image and its debug symbols for an architecture.

simple.remember: Check the actual selected settings and artifact identity before interpreting behavior.
simple.boundary: A serial number explains matching, but an iOS artifact also has target, action, configuration, platform, and architecture coordinates. Device arm64 and simulator arm64 are different variants. Matching symbols permit attribution; they do not prove a root cause. The supplied settings and UUIDs are invented.

sections.title: Name the symptom and the exact product
sections.html:
An artifact is an actual build product, such as an app bundle, executable, or symbol file. On Android you may trace Gradle inputs into an APK to explain a wrong application ID or missing resource. Use the same evidence habit on iOS. Target, scheme action, configuration, destination, environment, and installed bundle identity are separate coordinates. Choose one symptom: a scratch Sandbox Profile run selects the production branch, a resource lookup returns nil, or a crash stack lacks symbols. Write the expected behavior and identify the exact artifact you have. Do not let a familiar product name stand in for that identity.

Use SwiftUIWorkbench as the native scratch boundary and SwiftLanguageLab for host language fixtures. The command menu is an investigation aid, not an automated build or a record of executed commands. Inspect the project and verify its actual scheme/product names before substituting placeholders. Do not run company archive, signing, publishing, or cache-cleanup operations for this workshop. A missing native product is a precise limitation: source inspection can proceed, while artifact identity remains pending.

The supplied diagnostics are explicitly synthetic. Their setting values, product paths, UUIDs, and resource inventory are invented to exercise reasoning. Separate a source declaration from a resolved setting and from a packaged file. Each can falsify a different claim. A correct report says what layer was inspected and which next observation would distinguish the remaining explanations.

sections.title: Follow the selected action to its final settings
sections.html:
An effective setting is the final value after declarations and overrides are applied. In synthetic case A, the scheme is named Sandbox. Run uses Debug, while Profile uses Release. The xcconfig declares COURSE_SANDBOX, but the target's Release compilation-condition list replaces it with PROD. The effective excerpt therefore contains PROD, and the built Info.plist identifies example.course.workbench. The label Sandbox cannot select an environment by itself. Follow the action and configuration actually used; seeing a Debug branch tells you nothing about this Profile action's Release behavior.

Read the relevant target settings and xcconfig include chain first. Then inspect selected effective settings for the same scheme action, configuration, and destination. xcodebuild’s showBuildSettings does not compile an app, although a project or package may require resolution first; record that limitation if encountered. Retain only the bounded keys needed for this diagnosis, such as configuration, bundle identifier, module name, compilation conditions, optimization, and debug-information format. Do not paste an unfiltered environment or signing dump.

The smallest correction proposal would restore the intended effective condition through the owning target contract, then verify branch behavior and installation identity. This workshop requests diagnosis; it performs no configuration rewrite. If the inspected project has different actual names or action choices, use those observations instead of forcing it to match the synthetic case. Android build-type/flavor intuition helps ask questions, but there is no automatic one-to-one iOS variant object.

sections.title: Check packaging and lookup as two separate jobs
sections.html:
A resource owner is the target or bundle that packages and supplies a file. Synthetic case B has two separate faults. The source target processes bootstrap.json, but its resource bundle is absent from the app. The consumer also searches Bundle.main instead of the resource owner's bundle. A nil URL does not tell you which fault occurred. Inspect four links in the chain: the resource target declaration, the consumer's dependency, the packaged bundle, and the lookup accessor. The right accessor cannot find a bundle that was never packaged. Packaging the bundle does not make Bundle.main the correct lookup owner.

For an already built scratch artifact, inspect only its verified app directory and the expected resource-bundle location. Read the two relevant Info.plist identity fields with plutil. List the specific owning bundle rather than recursively dumping unrelated build products. A source JSON file, asset catalog, or privacy declaration present in the repository proves neither target membership nor the final artifact’s contents. Generation, localization, and extension membership add their own consumers.

If an app and widget both consume the resource, inspect each product. A host Swift package lookup test may prove its fixture bundle contract while the extension packaging still remains pending. Missing, malformed, unavailable, and unsupported-schema outcomes should stay distinct; do not turn every lookup or decode failure into an empty successful result. The investigation should identify the smallest affected target and the evidence needed before any fix is recommended.

sections.title: Match binary UUIDs before reading a crash address
sections.html:
A dSYM holds debug symbols for a particular built binary. A UUID helps identify the binary image for an architecture. In synthetic case C, the arm64 crash image and executable both have UUID 11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555. The offered dSYM has a different UUID. Matching names do not make its symbols suitable. Compare the crash's Binary Images entry, retained executable, and dSYM for the relevant architecture. Also check platform identity: device arm64 and simulator arm64 are different variants. The architecture string alone cannot prove the artifacts belong together.

Use dwarfdump’s UUID inspection on explicit verified scratch paths. Those commands inspect existing files; they do not create a build or reconstruct missing symbols. If the UUID disagrees, stop precise symbol attribution and locate the matching retained build artifact. A nearby version, a freshly rebuilt executable, or the same source revision under changed settings can still be wrong. Record the missing-artifact request without claiming the crash was symbolicated.

Once identity matches, follow the supported symbolication workflow and retain crash addresses, load information, tool version, and the resulting attribution. An optimized frame can be inlined or lack ordinary local variables. A named stack is evidence to analyze, not automatic proof of a root cause. Distinguish a language trap, resource termination, loader failure, and asynchronous wait before selecting a fix or recovery operation.

sections.title: Inspect a stopped value before executing debugger code
sections.html:
A breakpoint pauses a process at a chosen location. In a scratch counter, set a source breakpoint, record why the process stopped, and select the relevant thread and frame. A frame is one call's current execution context. Use frame variable to inspect a stored count, and identify the loaded image. If the breakpoint never resolves, consider mismatched symbols or source, optimization, a path that never ran, or attachment to the wrong process. Those explanations need different checks. Clearing global caches does not identify which one is true.

LLDB expression can execute code. Reading a computed label through expression may call a getter; invoking recordTap changes state. This is different from inspecting a stored value in the selected frame. Optimization can make even stored-value inspection incomplete, so label unavailable values honestly. Never dump credentials, request bodies, all environment variables, or unrelated signing settings into a course artifact.

Objective-C interoperability failures need another contract: a missing generated Swift header concerns module and target identity; an unrecognized selector concerns exposed signature and receiver lifetime; a nil imported object concerns nullability and failure handling. None is fixed by a dSYM alone. The synthetic excerpt gives expected reasoning, while an executed debugger observation requires a real stopped scratch process and an identified artifact.

sections.title: Write what each observation proves and what is missing
sections.html:
A diagnosis ledger is a short record that lets someone repeat your reasoning. Include the symptom, expected behavior, source evidence, resolved settings, actual artifact evidence, remaining explanations, and next check. Case A's Release override explains why the earlier Sandbox condition is absent. Case B requires both resource packaging and owner lookup checks. Case C's mismatched symbols block precise address attribution. Label each invented excerpt as synthetic. You can reproduce the reasoning and inspect existing scratch products without changing a client configuration.

Preserve build-versus-runtime limits. Effective settings do not prove the app was built. A built app does not prove installation or a particular interaction. Host fixture tests do not certify device signing, shared-container access, resource protection, or distribution. Read-only inspection of an existing archive supplies bounded artifact evidence, while submitting that archive is an entirely different operation.

A reviewer should be able to repeat the selected command with the verified scratch path and obtain the same relevant fields. If the product is unavailable, leave that row pending and state which native lab build step would produce it. Do not replace missing files with invented output from the supplied excerpts. Use this artifact to propose the smallest targeted verification or correction, with a reconstruction boundary and accountable owner if implementation is later requested.

exercise.brief: Explain the three invented failures. Inspect any available scratch settings or products read-only, and record actual observations separately from the supplied excerpts.
steps: Name the target, scheme action, configuration, destination, expected environment, and exact product available for inspection.
For case A, follow Profile to Release and explain how PROD replaces COURSE_SANDBOX. Choose only the relevant effective-setting keys to inspect.
For case B, check the resource target, consumer dependency, packaged owning bundle, and lookup accessor separately.
For case C, compare the crash, executable, and dSYM UUIDs and architecture. Stop precise attribution when the symbol UUID differs.
Write the exact inspected paths and observations in a diagnosis ledger. Leave unavailable product rows pending and name the smallest next check.
acceptance: Declarations, effective settings, artifact contents and runtime behavior are distinct.
The symbol mismatch blocks precise attribution until matching artifacts exist.
Resource packaging and lookup ownership are checked independently.
No company configuration, signing input, live account, cache or release action changes.
Every claimed command/build/debugger observation has actual execution evidence.
exercise.solution:
In case A, Profile selects Release, whose effective condition list contains PROD. The earlier COURSE_SANDBOX declaration was replaced. Check the final conditions and built bundle identity for those same coordinates. In case B, both the resource bundle's packaging and the lookup owner's accessor need correction; neither a source file nor a green host test proves app and extension contents. In case C, the offered dSYM's UUID differs from the crash image, so it cannot identify the function at that address. First find the matching retained binary and symbol artifact for the correct architecture and platform.

The worked ledger labels all three excerpts synthetic. A learner may append observed scratch settings or existing product fields after running the read-only menu, retaining exact paths and tool identity. If no product exists, its row remains pending rather than borrowing an unrelated client archive. The recommendation is a small targeted follow-up for the diagnosed layer; no fix, app build, symbolication, or release is implied by reading this answer.

quiz.question: A scheme named Sandbox uses a Release Profile action whose effective conditions contain only PROD. What determines the compiled branch?
options: The scheme’s display name
The effective conditions for the selected action/configuration/target
Any condition written in any xcconfig file
quiz.explanation: Compilation uses resolved target settings. The scheme label and overridden declarations do not establish the emitted branch.

quiz.question: The source resource exists but the app’s owning resource bundle is absent. Does switching to Bundle.module alone prove the lookup will work?
options: Yes, source presence guarantees packaging
Yes, the app’s main bundle owns all resources
No, bundle packaging and the correct owner lookup are independent requirements
quiz.explanation: The appropriate accessor cannot find a resource in a missing bundle. Verify the consumer graph and packaged artifact as well.

quiz.question: A dSYM has the right app name but a different UUID from the crash image. What is the next step?
options: Find the UUID and architecture matching artifact before precise symbolication
Use it and assume nearby source lines are equivalent
Rebuild any current source and treat the new symbols as original
quiz.explanation: UUID/architecture identify the relevant symbols. A familiar name or newly rebuilt product does not establish that identity.

workshops.title: Regression decisions: run the gate and explain its answer
workshops.summary: Run the host evaluator on four invented record sets. Calculate its percentiles, count every attempted outcome, and explain pass, regression, invalid preparation, and missing data without claiming device performance.

simple.story: You make practice cards for twenty-two parcel deliveries. Twenty cards say the parcel arrived and include a time. Two say the delivery timed out and have no arrival time. You can sort the twenty arrival times to describe completed deliveries. But if you throw away the timeout cards, the service looks more reliable than the cards say. Keep all twenty-two attempts when counting failures. These are invented cards for checking a rule. Running the rule correctly does not show that a real delivery service improved.
simple.meaning: The evaluator calculates completed-success latency separately from attempted-operation outcome rates. Timeout records remain in the attempts denominator without becoming latency samples. A synthetic gate pass proves policy behavior on supplied records, not a faster phone.

example.before: The invented candidate has 20 completed durations from 90 through 109 milliseconds. Its nearest-rank p95 is 108.
example.change: Append two distinct measured records with prepared true, outcome timeout, and null milliseconds.
example.after: There are 22 attempts and 20 completed samples. p95 stays 108, but 2/22 attempts timed out, about 9.09 percent. That exceeds the fixture's 5-percent absolute failure limit.

picture.caption: Two timeout records change the failure rate without changing the completed-duration percentile.

items.label: Add 2 timeouts
items.text: Their completed durations are null, so neither joins the latency sample list.

items.label: Count 22 attempts
items.text: Both timeouts remain among the attempted operations.

items.label: Check the policy
items.text: The synthetic failure rate is 2/22, above the 5-percent limit.

words.meaning: A program that applies declared acceptance rules to supplied records.
Here, the sorted completed value at one-based rank ceil(0.95 × sample count).
The middle sorted value, or the average of the two middle values for an even count.
The total group used when calculating a rate, such as all attempted operations.
Runs grouped under declared matching conditions, such as device, build, and fixture.
A run declared before measurement to prepare the experiment, not a label added afterward to hide a result.

simple.remember: A good completed time cannot erase a failed attempt.
simple.boundary: The cards explain arithmetic and denominators. They are synthetic, and matching labels cannot verify a real device or control thermal drift. p95 from 20 values is not a confidence interval or a stable fleet estimate. Preparation failures are planned operations that never began, so they need a separate rate.

sections.title: Keep collecting measurements separate from evaluating them
sections.html:
A gate applies declared rules to records you give it. It does not collect those records. This workshop runs MeasurementLab's real host evaluator against deliberately invented inputs. The program uses only Node's built-in modules and has no network dependency. Like an Android benchmark comparison, its answer depends on how the operation and experiment were defined first. A threshold cannot repair a poorly defined measurement. Running this evaluator establishes what its policy does with these records. It supplies no evidence that a phone improved, that Instruments captured a trace, or that a learner completed a native exercise.

The metric is lower-is-better elapsed milliseconds from immediately before a synchronous map to after its returned value. Baseline and candidate records identify revision and a matching cohort: device label, OS, toolchain, configuration, fixture, preparation, cache policy, instrumentation, and metric identifier. The supplied labels are synthetic. When using actual experiments, obtain these fields from the recorded setup and preserve the raw artifacts rather than retroactively making mismatched runs look comparable.

Correctness is a hard prerequisite. Each version declares its independent contract result. The evaluator requires pass before considering latency, but the declaration is not authenticated proof: attach the actual expected-value tests and results. A faster candidate that changes ordering, drops rows, suppresses errors, or publishes stale ownership fails the product question regardless of its timing.

sections.title: Keep successful, failed, and unstarted records distinct
sections.html:
A run record describes one planned operation. It has a unique ID, a phase chosen beforehand, preparation state, outcome, and duration. A completed success needs finite, nonnegative milliseconds. Failure, timeout, and cancellation have null completed duration because no completed-success latency was recorded. These attempted operations still count when computing the outcome rate. For example, 20 completed successes and 2 timeouts make 22 attempts, not 20. Keep a timeout as a timeout: neither calling it a slow success nor removing it from the failure rate preserves the record's meaning.

Preparation failures use prepared false, outcome not-run, and null duration. They are counted among planned measurement records but do not enter attempted-operation latency or failure denominators. The policy separately limits preparation failure rate. This distinction prevents a broken fixture from being reported as a product regression while still exposing a failing harness. A declared warmup must complete successfully before measured records and match the policy’s count. Late relabeling of an inconvenient sample as warmup is invalid input.

The policy fixes minimum completed samples, warmup count, absolute p95 budget, allowed relative p95 increase, absolute failure rate, allowed failure-rate increase, preparation-failure limit, and an accountable reviewer. The fixture numbers are illustrative, not recommendations for an app. Real budgets depend on user requirements, baseline variability, repeatability, and the particular environment. Setting the budget after seeing the candidate defeats the decision contract.

sections.title: Calculate p95 and median from small sorted lists
sections.html:
An estimator is the rule used to turn samples into a reported number. This evaluator uses nearest-rank p95. Sort a copy of the completed durations, calculate ceil(0.95 × n), and read that one-based rank. Subtract one only when using a zero-based array index. For 20 ordered values from 100 to 119, rank 19 gives p95 118. The conventional median averages the two middle values, 109 and 110, to give 109.5. Nearest-rank p50 would give 109, so it is a different rule. Sorting a copy keeps the raw input order intact for later review.

The supplied pass candidate has values 90 through 109, yielding median 99.5 and p95 108. These are arithmetic facts about invented arrays. Twenty samples permit this calculation, but the result is not a confidence interval or a stable fleet tail estimate. Repeated correlated observations on one warmed runner need their own interpretation. Do not average device p95 values or add phase p95 values and rename the result an end-to-end p95.

A zero baseline needs an explicit rule because percentage increase is undefined. The evaluator leaves relativeIncrease null; zero-to-zero can satisfy the comparison, while positive candidate latency fails the relative-growth guard. This is a deterministic policy choice for the teaching harness. If zero indicates timer resolution or a broken measurement in your actual experiment, classify and investigate that condition before treating the comparison as meaningful.

sections.title: Run the host tests and all four fixture commands
sections.html:
An exit code is the number a command returns to describe its outcome. From the course directory, run node --test labs/MeasurementLab/test-evaluate.mjs. Then run node labs/MeasurementLab/evaluate.mjs labs/MeasurementLab/fixtures/pass.json. Repeat with regression, invalid-preparation, and missing-data in place of pass in the supplied filename. Each command writes a JSON report and returns a distinct exit code. A nonzero code for a deliberately failing fixture is an expected demonstration of that policy outcome. Record it and its reasons rather than treating it as a failed teaching check to hide.

Pass exits 0. Regression exits 1. Invalid preparation exits 2. Missing data exits 3. Additional guards use 4 for incompatible cohorts, 5 for failed correctness, and 6 for invalid data or a CLI file/JSON error. The test file asserts both the exported function result and the actual CLI status for the four main fixtures. It also covers percentile arithmetic, raw-order preservation, timeouts, metadata mismatch, malformed samples, duplicate IDs, warmup ordering, allowed preparation exclusions, and zero baselines.

Read the full report rather than only its status. It retains record counts, warmups, planned measurements, invalid preparation, attempts, outcome counts, completed-sample count, rates, median, p95, range, and the comparison. File and JSON errors emit no pass report. No script in this lab updates client source, a baseline file, a course progress record, or a release system.

sections.title: Explain pass, regression, and an undecidable experiment
sections.html:
A pass means these records meet this declared policy. The pass fixture has baseline p95 118 and candidate p95 108. Its synthetic absolute budget is 130, and its allowed relative increase is 10 percent. The cohorts match, and both independent correctness declarations say pass. These inputs therefore satisfy the gate. The answer supports review of this experiment's records. It neither releases a product nor establishes statistical confidence. First keep the arithmetic check separate from the question of whether actual measurements and correctness evidence are trustworthy.

The regression fixture changes candidate values to 120 through 139, giving p95 138. It fails the absolute budget and increases p95 by approximately 16.95 percent against 118. Keep both reasons visible. The invalid-preparation fixture completes its warmup but marks every planned measured candidate operation not-run. Its preparation-failure rate is 100 percent, so product performance remains undecidable. The missing-data fixture claims one completed operation without a duration; the evaluator refuses to fabricate or interpolate that observation.

Choose a bounded next action. For regression, inspect correctness and cohort records, retain the candidate/baseline artifacts, and confirm the suspected mechanism under the declared rerun policy. For invalid preparation, repair the fixture or runner before a comparable measurement. For missing data, recover the original result record or rerun a declared batch; do not copy a neighboring duration. Limit retries and retain first failures instead of repeatedly running until the gate happens to pass.

sections.title: Name who reviews the result and what remains unproved
sections.html:
A guardrail is a declared limit that can reject an otherwise promising candidate. Outcome-rate guardrails still matter when completed latency improves. With 20 completed candidate samples and 2 extra timeouts, there are 22 attempts and 2 failed outcomes. Completed p95 can stay unchanged while the evaluator rejects the failure rate. A product with many intentional cancellations may need a different rule, but that rule needs an explicit decision. Removing cancelled attempts after collection would change the denominator to make the result look better. Review the policy and the raw records together.

Matched cohort metadata is necessary, yet not sufficient to guarantee a well-controlled experiment. This program does not verify device truth, measure thermal drift, pair alternating samples, estimate uncertainty, collect hitches, or inspect memory and energy. Keep those evidence rows separate. An absolute budget represents a product requirement; the relative guard detects deterioration against the chosen control. Both depend on the validity of their inputs.

The handoff names the policy owner, estimator, exclusions, raw artifact locations, conditions, tested behavior, and pending evidence. Any threshold update requires a documented decision and comparable new baseline evidence. A plain synthetic pass should remain a synthetic pass when incorporated into the course. Use the gate to make uncertainty and the next action visible, while preserving independent human review for adoption and recovery.

exercise.brief: Run the evaluator's tests and four fixture files. Explain each exit code, then add two invented timeouts to check the difference between completed samples and attempts.
steps: Run the host tests. Record the actual Node version, command, exit code, and test summary.
Run pass.json, regression.json, invalid-preparation.json, and missing-data.json. Record each status, exit code, and reason.
Calculate p95 and median yourself for the pass and regression arrays before comparing them with the reports.
In a scratch copy or an imported evaluate call, add two distinct timeout records with prepared true and null milliseconds. Calculate 2/22 and check that the completed p95 is unchanged.
Name a bounded next step for regression, invalid preparation, and missing data. Keep device observations and product decisions as separate pending evidence.
acceptance: Pass/regression/invalid-preparation/missing-data are demonstrated by actual program execution.
Twenty-value p95 uses rank nineteen and even-sample median uses the middle pair.
Timeouts remain in attempts and never enter completed-success latency.
Invalid/missing/cohort/correctness conditions cannot silently pass.
Fixture timings and budgets stay labeled synthetic; no baseline or release is automatically changed.
exercise.solution:
The 20 baseline values from 100 through 119 give median 109.5 and p95 118. The pass candidate's 90 through 109 give median 99.5 and p95 108. The regression candidate's 120 through 139 give median 129.5 and p95 138, exceeding both 130 and the allowed 10-percent increase. Invalid preparation gives a preparation-failure rate of one and no valid measured candidate attempt. Missing data claims a completion without its duration, so the evaluator rejects it. These are predicted answers for invented fixtures. Record your actual command outputs to verify the program agrees.

For the additional schedule, append two distinct measurement records with prepared true, timeout outcome, and null milliseconds. The twenty completed candidate samples still yield p95 108, but twenty-two attempts now include two timeouts. The rate is about 9.09 percent, exceeding the synthetic absolute 5-percent limit and the allowed 2-percentage-point increase. The test suite exercises this mutation. A reviewer preserves those failed outcomes, diagnoses under a bounded protocol, and collects appropriate device evidence before making a product decision.

quiz.question: Twenty successes and two timeouts have which outcome denominator?
options: Twenty because only successes count
Twenty-two attempted operations, with twenty completed latency samples
Two because the gate cares only about failures
quiz.explanation: Timeouts remain attempted failures while completed-success latency uses the twenty successful observations.

quiz.question: A candidate fixture fails to prepare before every measured operation. What should happen?
options: Approve if the warmup was fast
Report a product regression with invented durations
Classify invalid preparation and repair the experiment before comparing latency
quiz.explanation: The product operation never ran. Harness preparation must be made comparable before performance can be decided.

quiz.question: What does a synthetic pass from this evaluator establish?
options: The declared policy accepts the supplied records under its arithmetic and validation rules
Representative device energy improved
Automatic readiness to release the application
quiz.explanation: The program evaluates records. It does not collect or authenticate measurements, establish uncertainty, or perform delivery.

workshops.title: Platform decisions: compare costs, owners, and adoption
workshops.summary: Practice a multi-team read-contract proposal. Compare alternatives and estimated costs, assign owners, define adoption and recovery checks, and distinguish a local implementation from independently verified organizational results.

simple.story: Three households consider building a shared tool shed. It could reduce repeated upkeep, but building it takes time. Someone must maintain it, each household must learn to use it, and a household with different needs may keep its own cupboard. Finishing the shed does not prove everyone uses it. The group tries it with one small job first, checks the upkeep, and agrees who can stop the trial. They also decide what to remove if it works, and what to remove if it fails.
simple.meaning: A platform proposal needs more than one working adapter. It must compare options, fund adoption, assign decision rights, allow justified exceptions, and plan recovery and retirement. Local test results and cross-team adoption require different evidence.

example.before: Synthetic Option A costs 4 engineer-weeks initially and 3 owner-days per month. Option B costs 10 weeks and 2 owner-days per month.
example.change: Assume one engineer-week equals 5 comparable owner-days. Compare B's extra initial cost with its estimated monthly saving.
example.after: B adds (10 - 4) × 5 = 30 days and saves an estimated 1 day per month. Simple payback is 30 months before training, parallel maintenance, or other extra costs. These are planning assumptions, not observed savings.

picture.caption: Three proposed options have different scope and synthetic costs; each needs evidence before expansion.

items.label: A: Local adapters
items.text: Keep implementations local: estimate 4 weeks initially and 3 maintenance days monthly.

items.label: B: Shared contract
items.text: Use native adapters under common rules: estimate 10 weeks and 2 monthly days.

items.label: C: Shared engine
items.text: Share execution too: estimate 22 weeks and 4 monthly days, with added runtime coupling.

items.label: Review the pilot
items.text: Check real adoption, cost, ownership, and recovery before claiming benefit.

words.meaning: An implementation that connects a shared behavior contract to a platform's own APIs.
A feature or team-owned component that uses the proposed contract.
A required behavior that must stay true across supported implementations.
A consumer actually using and verifying the agreed contract, beyond adding a dependency.
A recorded, owned reason one consumer needs a different contract, with tests and a review date.
Removing a superseded or rejected path after compatibility and recovery checks permit it.

simple.remember: A working local change, an adopted platform, and a measured benefit are three separate claims.
simple.boundary: The shed explains cost and shared responsibility, not equivalent iOS and Android execution. Estimates need observed review, proposed owners need confirmed acceptance, and publication is not adoption. An installed-client flag cannot downgrade a binary. Course artifacts do not prove organizational approval, product improvement, or professional readiness.

sections.title: Separate one working adapter from a multi-team strategy
sections.html:
A shared contract states the behavior several implementations must provide. In this invented scenario, three product teams need account-safe one-shot reads while iOS transports coexist. Android uses a different coroutine and transport implementation. Your Android leadership experience helps with the ownership question: who may accept an answer during a transition? Existing clients remain installed, a service owns authorization, and changing account ownership must reject stale final results. The proposal covers read operations. It supplies no replay of booking writes and no database migration. Keep those boundaries clear before choosing shared infrastructure.

A staff-sized contribution can own one iOS consumer seam: characterize existing errors and cancellation, implement a bounded adapter, prove stale results cannot commit, validate its artifact, and rehearse recovery. A principal-sized exercise connects that work to a multi-team strategy: what product contract is shared, which implementations remain native, who pays adoption cost, how exceptions are handled, and who funds maintenance and retirement. The distinction is responsibility scope and evidence, not more obscure syntax or an automatic title.

The supplied platform-decision.json is an invented review record. Its roles, estimates, targets, and dates describe proposed accountability rather than company maintainers or approvals. No platform rollout, customer improvement, or team adoption is claimed. Use it to practice deciding under uncertainty and asking what evidence would overturn the recommendation.

sections.title: Compare the options and calculate estimated payback
sections.html:
An option is one possible way to solve the declared problem. Option A keeps local adapters and publishes common behavior fixtures. Its invented estimate is 4 engineer-weeks initially and 3 owner-days of maintenance per month. It asks consumers to change less, while duplicated implementation and review continue. A may be appropriate when shared failures are rare or consumers need different behavior. Publishing fixtures gives teams an input to use; it does not show that they adopted the rules. Compare this smaller option with the larger proposals and with leaving the system as it is.

Option B defines a shared product contract with native iOS and Android adapters and staged adoption. The estimate is ten engineer-weeks plus two owner-days per month. It standardizes outcome, cancellation, ownership, and evidence requirements while retaining platform execution details. Its cost includes adapters, parallel paths during migration, training, consumer changes, and compatibility fixtures. A shared protocol does not eliminate maintenance or guarantee the two runtimes behave identically.

Option C builds one execution engine across platforms. The estimate is twenty-two engineer-weeks plus four owner-days per month. It could reduce some repeated logic, but introduces interop, lifecycle, debugging, resource, packaging, and deployment coupling. Treat these estimates as planning assumptions, not observed savings. Include feature opportunity cost and corrective delivery, state who bears them, and compare all options against leaving the system alone. Provisionally test B only if a pilot can establish useful shared invariants and a plausible cost advantage.

Write the estimated arithmetic where someone can check it. Assume one engineer-week equals five comparable owner-days. B needs six more weeks than A, so its extra initial cost is 6 × 5 = 30 days. Its estimated maintenance saving is 3 - 2 = 1 day per month. Simple undiscounted payback is therefore 30 months. Training, parallel maintenance, corrective work, and discounting can lengthen it. The conversion also fails if the compared owners' capacity is not comparable. C costs more than A both initially and monthly, so these numbers alone cannot justify it as an engineering-time saving. It needs another explicit product or risk benefit. The arithmetic may favor A or no change. A pilot must collect evidence that could overturn the choice; a preference for sharing is not evidence of return on investment.

sections.title: Make the iOS implementation independently checkable
sections.html:
A seam is the connection where a consumer selects and calls an implementation. The iOS adapter owner traces the established composition and credential seam rather than inventing a new global session. Its contract states request start, one terminal success or error, cancellation, captured account epoch, and who may make the final synchronous state change. Each request captures its selected implementation before it suspends. If an old shared resource must remain alive until active operations finish, track those operations and define the promotion checks. Calling a gateway a snapshot does not implement that draining rule. A reviewer needs observable behavior, not just a new name.

Characterization fixtures cover full-value success, empty success, ordinary remote failure, caller cancellation followed by late success or ordinary failure, supersession, and A-to-B-to-A account ownership. The repository contract in lesson 020 checks caller cancellation on the throwing path, otherwise preserving the remote failure. Successful stale results use account and request guards. Shared product outcome rules need not force Android and iOS to use the same exception classes or scheduler.

The staff handoff includes executed fixture results, source/target membership, matching build and runtime coordinates, a narrow interaction check, and pending device/artifact rows. It identifies the existing and candidate resource lifetimes and future-operation rollback. These artifacts make the pilot defensible, but do not prove another team adopted it. A strong local implementation is necessary evidence for expansion, while the principal exercise must still settle cross-team constraints and operational ownership.

sections.title: Give every adoption and stop decision an owner
sections.html:
An accountable owner has a specific deliverable and authority to make its decision. These are proposed roles in the exercise. The mobile platform lead owns the contract, funding, exception record, and migration-debt deadline. The iOS lead owns credential and session integration plus final-result tests; the Android lead owns equivalent native behavior. Consumer leads own loading, failure, and selection behavior and their adoption schedules. The service lead owns authorization, response compatibility, and write reconciliation. Release and observability leads own installed cohorts, matching artifacts, comparable metrics, and the authority to pause expansion. Confirmed ownership would need evidence outside this invented record.

These roles need explicit deliverables and decision rights. A reviewer can challenge a privacy field without becoming the unnamed owner of all security risk. A consumer team can request an exception when its stream semantics differ from a one-shot read. The exception records the reason, affected contract, local owner, compensating tests, cost, and next review. It is not a silent fork or a blanket mandate to migrate every API.

Set a bounded pilot: one read consumer per platform, with a small number of consenting synthetic team roles in the exercise. Expansion requires evidence and an agreed budget for the next wave. If a team cannot allocate adoption time, adjust the sequence or fund assistance rather than counting a published guideline as adoption. The principal decision should explain how decentralized consumer work remains compatible while one accountable owner maintains the shared contract.

sections.title: Count verified consumers and include exceptions
sections.html:
An adoption gate is a stated check required before the next stage. First characterize existing adapters with independent expected outcomes. Then pilot with behavior parity, controlled in-flight selection, app and consumer artifacts, and representative interaction checks. Expansion needs comparable outcomes and observed maintenance cost. Retirement needs migrated supported consumers or recorded exceptions, completed old operations, compatibility for installed clients, and a signed decision record from the accountable roles. A review date asks people to inspect that evidence; it does not remove the checks. These stages need independent records of what teams actually did.

Measure adoption as eligible consumers adopting the agreed contract, split by team and platform, with exceptions visible in the denominator. Count an implementation only when its consumer behavior and required artifacts pass, not when a dependency is added. Correctness metrics count controlled schedules and stale commits. Operational outcomes use attempted reads in a matching build/cohort/time window, including failure and cancellation. Success-only latency can conceal a worsening product.

Cost metrics include adapter maintenance, incident handling, onboarding, and repeated review effort in a declared window. Compare observed cost with the planning estimates before expanding. Device latency, error rate, and release evidence remain pending until collected. A synthetic gate pass or hypothetical cost table cannot become customer benefit in the portfolio. Define the smallest next observation that can falsify the recommendation, such as incompatible cancellation ownership or no meaningful reduction in repeated maintenance.

sections.title: Keep recovery possible and remove the correct old path
sections.html:
Containment limits further harm while a problem is investigated. It can select the existing adapter for future reads only when the installed binary contains and honors that choice. Requests already running keep their chosen adapter under the switching policy. Keep their session alive while they depend on it. A timed-out write is different: its server effect may be unknown, so replaying it through another transport could repeat the action. Service authorization and any idempotency or reconciliation rules stay with their established owners. This read-only pilot needs a precise future-operation recovery rule, not an assumed universal rollback.

Remote configuration may be unavailable before startup completes. A launch failure on that path can require a corrective binary and compatible service behavior for older clients, not an assumed flag reversal. Pausing a phased release limits further progression but does not downgrade installed apps. Keep reconstructible prior graph inputs and matching artifacts as delivery evidence, while acknowledging that developer reconstruction is different from installed-client rollback.

On successful adoption, retire the old adapter and temporary switching machinery after supported consumers, exceptions, resource draining, and recovery review permit it. If the experiment is rejected, retire the candidate instead and restore the supported old contract. Give debt an owner and review window; the synthetic example uses six weeks to revisit it, not as an automatic removal deadline. Persistent-format changes would require a separate compatibility and repair design beyond this read-only pilot.

sections.title: Challenge one assumption and revise the decision
sections.html:
A critique rubric lists concrete things a reviewer can check. This one has six dimensions: precise contract, viable alternatives, cost model, accountable owners, adoption evidence, and recovery plus retirement. Score each 0 when missing, 1 when proposed but unverified, and 2 when supported by a reproducible artifact appropriate to its scope. A proposed role without confirmed acceptance is still 1. A cost estimate helps planning, but it is not observed cost. Use the separate scores to locate missing evidence; they are not a measure of professional title or readiness.

The reviewer then changes one assumption: a consumer emits cached and fresh values, configuration cannot load, an extension shares durable state, or a team cannot adopt this quarter. Ask which contract, option, owner, gate, and cost change. A one-shot async adapter cannot silently absorb stream replay; a single-process actor cannot provide an interprocess transaction; a plan that survives only unanimous simultaneous adoption needs a better compatibility seam.

Finish with a conditional decision: accept a bounded pilot, revise the proposal, or defer expansion pending named evidence. Record a dissent and the evidence that would resolve it. Do not sum rubric scores into a principal-readiness certification. A course review can demonstrate reasoning and suggest a supervised next responsibility; sustained independent delivery, cross-team adoption, and operational accountability require actual evidence beyond this exercise.

exercise.brief: Propose a small cross-team read pilot. Supply a checkable iOS handoff and a separate ownership and adoption record, then revise the proposal when one assumption changes.
steps: Write the shared behaviors that must stay true. State which execution, cancellation, and lifecycle details remain native to each platform.
Compare A, B, C, and no change using the invented cost assumptions. Calculate B's 30-month simple payback and include work deferred to fund the pilot.
Assign proposed owners, deliverables, and stop authority. Record one justified exception for a consumer with a different contract.
Define the checks for characterization, pilot, adoption, and retirement. Count eligible consumers and keep exceptions visible in the adoption total.
Rehearse selecting the old path for future reads and a failure before configuration loads. Explain which path is removed after success and which after rejecting the experiment.
Score the six review dimensions using proposed versus reproduced evidence. Change one adoption or recovery assumption and name the next bounded responsibility.
acceptance: Staff implementation evidence and principal adoption/accountability work are distinct.
Options include costs, constraints and a condition that reverses the recommendation.
Owners, stop authority and exception review are explicit without invented company approvals.
Installed-client and ambiguous-write recovery limits are respected.
Successful deprecation removes the old path; rejected experimentation removes the candidate.
Metrics distinguish adoption, correctness, product outcomes and cost; synthetic values remain labeled.
exercise.solution:
The worked decision permits only a conditional Option B pilot: one read consumer per platform, using native adapters with common outcome and ownership fixtures. The staff contribution owns the iOS connection and controlled success, error, cancellation, and account-change results. A separate principal-scope proposal names the cross-team owner, funds the proposed work, and defines exception review. Compare B's estimated 10 engineer-weeks with A's 4 and C's 22. Under the stated comparable-day assumption, B's simple payback against A is 30 months before extra costs. That may favor a smaller option unless the pilot demonstrates a justified benefit. No observed savings or confirmed organizational adoption are supplied.

A consumer that emits cache then refresh receives an explicit stream-contract exception instead of pretending the one-shot adapter is equivalent. Adoption counts eligible consumers and unresolved exceptions by platform. Expansion waits for independent contract results, representative artifacts, attempted-read guardrails, and a maintenance review. Recovery selects the old path for future supported reads while preserving active resources; a pre-configuration fault can need corrective delivery. Successful adoption retires the old path after evidence review, while rejection retires the candidate. Rubric scores remain proposed where artifacts are pending, leading to a bounded pilot decision rather than a title or production-impact claim.

quiz.question: Which responsibility expands the exercise from a staff seam to a principal strategy?
options: Replacing every native API with the same library
Owning cross-team adoption, funding, exceptions and retirement evidence
Knowing more framework trivia
quiz.explanation: Principal scope connects technical work to coordinated adoption and durable accountability; code breadth alone does not establish it.

quiz.question: After the candidate is adopted successfully, which path is normally retired after evidence review?
options: The adopted candidate regardless of consumer state
Every route immediately on the review date
The old path and temporary switching machinery, subject to compatibility and recovery gates
quiz.explanation: Successful adoption retires superseded debt. A rejected experiment instead removes its candidate; dates do not bypass evidence.

quiz.question: A published guideline and a synthetic gate pass justify which claim?
options: A proposed strategy with bounded fixture evidence, while adoption and product outcomes remain pending
Observed company-wide maintenance savings
Automatic principal readiness
quiz.explanation: Artifacts can support a proposal. Cross-team adoption, sustained outcomes and readiness require appropriate independent evidence.
